documents.title: Regulation for the Use of Generative AI Systems with Institutional Data
documents.summary: A university regulation on using generative AI with institutional data. It welcomes exploration but sorts tools by data classification level, restricts protected data to vetted tools, and covers vendor contracts and procurement. It says nothing about classroom or coursework use.
documents.stance_why: The regulation says the university "allows Generative AI tools to be utilized effectively" and "encourages exploration", and allows any tool for public data, but conditions use on data level and vetted tools, so permit with conditions.

units.why: The purpose clause sets the institution-wide framing: the regulation exists so the university "allows Generative AI tools to be utilized effectively" while protecting data. A purpose statement for everyone, so P56 (general, informs).
units.anchor: the University allows Generative AI tools to be utilized effectively without compromising the integrity

units.why: The purpose also names what the regulation is for: guidelines that "safeguard academic integrity, protect intellectual property, and ensure compliance". This states scope and principles, so P56 rather than a specific integrity rule.
units.anchor: guidelines that safeguard academic integrity, protect intellectual property, and ensure compliance with legal and regulatory

units.why: The sentence defines generative AI ("a type of artificial intelligence that produces new content"), which sets what the regulation covers, so P61.
units.anchor: Generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that produces new content

units.why: The university "encourages exploration of these products or services", a welcoming default stance toward generative AI, so P02 with modality should and unit stance encourage.
units.anchor: East Carolina University encourages exploration of these products or services

units.why: Individuals "must remain cognizant of data being provided to these tools": a duty to be careful with data entered into AI, so P50 (protect data) with must.
units.anchor: individuals must remain cognizant of data being provided to these tools

units.why: Users must "abide by copyright laws, compliance regulations" and the codes of conduct when using AI. Copyright is the specific named concern, so P52 rather than the generic P50.
units.anchor: abide by copyright laws, compliance regulations, Employee Code of Conduct, and Student Code of Conduct

units.why: Violators "will be subject to the penalties outlined in" the employee, faculty and student conduct processes, so violations go through existing conduct processes (P36). No concrete penalties are given, so not P37.
units.anchor: found to be in violation of this regulation will be subject to the penalties outlined

units.why: For Level 1 public data "Any generative AI product or service is allowed", a permissive rule on which tools may be used. It is about tool and data choice, so P50 with may.
units.anchor: Any generative AI product or service is allowed.

units.why: For protected data "Only generative AI products or services that are run offline and locally on ECU managed devices or are listed" are authorized: a restriction to vetted tools, so P50 with must.
units.anchor: generative AI products or services that are run offline and locally on ECU managed devices

units.why: The text warns that other tools "could violate state or federal statutes such as HIPAA and FERPA", explaining the data restriction. A fact informing P50.
units.anchor: could violate state or federal statutes such as HIPAA and FERPA

units.why: "Passphrases must never be used" with AI not integrated with single sign-on is a data-protection prohibition (P50, must-not).
units.anchor: Passphrases must never be used with generative AI products or services

units.why: "Never share any sensitive, personal, or institutional data" with AI tools that are "public facing" protects personal data: P50, must-not.
units.anchor: Never share any sensitive, personal, or institutional data

units.why: Under "Recommended Practices", users should "Review and be familiar with ECU’s data classification standards", which supports correct tool choice by data level (P50, should).
units.anchor: Review and be familiar with ECU’s data classification standards

units.why: Those who work with institutional data "must be aware of HIPAA, FERPA, GDPR, GLBA": a duty to know legal data obligations when using AI, P50 with must.
units.anchor: must be aware of HIPAA, FERPA, GDPR, GLBA, and other federal, state, or university regulations

units.why: The passage says AI is "a prominent driver of phishing scams" and that security practices "must be followed". This is an AI-enabled security risk, not bias or environment (P53), and no other type covers phishing, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: ITCS Information Security Best Practices must be followed and any suspicious messages reported
units.uncovered_note: AI-enabled phishing and information-security practices: follow ITCS best practices and report suspicious messages.

units.why: "The approval of a tool does not override any governing data laws" and a data steward, IRB or Data Use Agreement can bar AI use. Deferring to IRB and data-use-agreement rules matches P62.
units.anchor: you may not use generative AI tools even if they are approved herein

units.why: Acquisition "must comply with the Software and Data Collection Services Acquisition Regulation": institutional review of AI purchasing, so P65.
units.anchor: acquisition of generative AI products or services must comply with the Software and Data Collection

units.why: Approved vendors "must adhere to security industry best practices" to protect university data, a vendor-agreement data-protection condition, P65.
units.anchor: security industry best practices to safeguard and protect any data, documents, files, and other materials

units.why: Security obligations "must also apply to the generative AI models trained with university data": a condition on vendors who train on university data, P65.
units.anchor: must also apply to the generative AI models trained with university data

units.why: "Available and approved software ... can be found via" a licensed software site, pointing users to vetted tools (P50, informs).
units.anchor: and approved software at the University can be found via the Licensed ECU Software Downloads

units.why: "No exceptions to this regulation will be approved until a contract is in place" with the AI parent company is a contract-review rule for AI vendors, P65.
units.anchor: No exceptions to this regulation will be approved until a contract is in place

units.why: "Any procurement ... must go through the Technology Purchase Process" is a separate procurement rule from the contract rule above; P65.
units.anchor: Any procurement of a generative AI product or service must go through the Technology Purchase

units.why: "All faculty, staff, and students are required to follow" the regulation states who it binds, a scope statement, P56.
units.anchor: All faculty, staff, and students are required to follow the Institutional Data and AI regulation.

documents.unit: Office for Faculty Excellence / ECU Libraries
documents.title: Generative AI in the Classroom & Research: Classroom Best Practices
documents.summary: A library guide for faculty on classroom AI. It leaves the decision to instructors, supplies three syllabus-statement templates, ties misuse and uncited use to academic integrity, and adds notes on copyright, hallucination and sample AI assignments.
documents.stance_why: The guide says "faculty have the ability to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence may be used" and offers three templates to choose from, so it sets no stance itself and delegates, with tiers listed.

units.why: The guide says faculty "have the ability to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence may be used in the classroom", leaving the decision to each instructor: P04.
units.anchor: ability to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence may be used in the classroom

units.why: "Policies should be in keeping with the University's Academic Integrity policies" constrains instructor-set rules. It is a bound on instructor discretion, so P04 rather than P36.
units.anchor: Policies should be in keeping with the University's Academic Integrity policies

units.why: The guide offers "three scenarios and examples of syllabus language faculty can choose from" (prohibited, prior permission, acknowledgement), a menu of named categories: P05.
units.anchor: three scenarios and examples of syllabus language faculty can choose from

units.why: "using an AI tool, if prohibited by the instructor, is considered an academic integrity violation" classifies prohibited use as misconduct: P36.
units.anchor: using an AI tool, if prohibited by the instructor, is considered an academic integrity violation

units.why: Using another's "language, structure, ideas" without citing "is considered plagiarism"; it applies the plagiarism definition to uncited work, so P36.
units.anchor: without citing the work appropriately is considered plagiarism

units.why: "We strongly recommend faculty remind their students to always cite when using any AI tool": an instructor-addressed recommendation about citation, P24.
units.anchor: We strongly recommend faculty remind their students to always cite when using any AI tool

units.why: "even if permitted by the instructor, using an AI tool without properly citing its use is also plagiarism" makes non-disclosure the violation: P28.
units.anchor: by the instructor, using an AI tool without properly citing its use is also plagiarism

units.why: The office created "Academic Syllabus Statements" and "faculty resources" for instructors to add to syllabi. This is support for faculty, P63 (not P09, which would require a statement).
units.anchor: has created several Academic Syllabus Statements that you can add to your syllabi

units.why: "Please modify these statements to suit the needs of your course" lets each instructor adapt the rule, P04.
units.anchor: Please modify these statements to suit the needs of your course.

units.why: Template 1 says "Students are not allowed to use advanced automated tools" on assignments, a default ban on graded work: P01.
units.anchor: Students are not allowed to use advanced automated tools

units.why: "complete each assignment without substantive assistance from others, including automated tools" bars AI from doing the submitted work. P19 chosen because it treats the tool as a source of assistance on submitted work; P45 (AI as collaborator) fits less since it is a ban, not a collaboration rule.
units.anchor: complete each assignment without substantive assistance from others, including automated tools

units.why: Template 2 allows AI "if instructor permission is obtained in advance", so students must ask first: P10.
units.anchor: on assignments in this course if instructor permission is obtained in advance

units.why: "Unless given permission to use those tools" students complete work without assistance: a fallback when no permission is granted, P06.
units.anchor: to use those tools, each student is expected to complete each assignment without substantive assistance

units.why: If permission is granted, tools "must be properly documented and credited": disclosure with each submission, P24.
units.anchor: they must be properly documented and credited

units.why: Students "should seek out the appropriate source (e.g., MLA, APA, etc..) and cite in the most correct format", a citation-format instruction for AI use: P24 (it does not require prompt or model details, so not P25).
units.anchor: cite in the most correct format according to the style guide

units.why: Students "must also include a brief (2-3 sentences) description of how they used the tool": a short written account of AI use, closest to P26 (reflections) rather than P24.
units.anchor: students must also include a brief (2-3 sentences) description of how they used the tool

units.why: Template 3 allows AI "if that use is properly documented and credited", a permissive default with a disclosure condition: P02.
units.anchor: on assignments in this course if that use is properly documented and credited

units.why: The guide suggests assignments like "Have students use an AI-powered image recognition tool to classify images", building course work around AI tools: P35.
units.anchor: Have students use an AI-powered image recognition tool to classify images

units.why: "These assignments can help students develop a better understanding of how AI works" and improve skills, so the guide frames AI assignments as teaching AI as a skill: P44.
units.anchor: These assignments can help students develop a better understanding of how AI works

units.why: In the ChatGPT-generated text reproduced on the page, "AI-powered tools can be used to grade assignments and provide feedback". It describes instructor use of AI for teaching work, so P59, but it is quoted AI output with no endorsement, hence informs.
units.anchor: AI-powered tools can be used to grade assignments and provide feedback to students

units.why: The reproduced ChatGPT answer says AI should be used "in a responsible and transparent way" with ethical implications considered; a general ethics caution, P53.
units.anchor: carefully consider the potential ethical implications of using AI in education

units.why: Under "Unfair Advantage" the reproduced answer says AI tools "could lead to academic dishonesty"; a named harm, so P53.
units.anchor: could lead to academic dishonesty, and ultimately undermine the integrity of the educational system

units.why: "AI tools may require access to student data, which raises privacy concerns" in the reproduced answer: P50 informs.
units.anchor: AI tools may require access to student data, which raises privacy concerns.

units.why: The reproduced answer says models "can perpetuate biases that exist in the data": bias, P53.
units.anchor: they can perpetuate biases that exist in the data

units.why: "Citing ChatGPT and other generative AI will allow your work to remain transparent": advice that AI use be cited, P24 (should).
units.anchor: Citing ChatGPT and other generative AI will allow your work to remain transparent

units.why: "If generative AI is used in research, best practice would dictate to mention the use of this tool in the narrative" concerns AI in research writing: P62.
units.anchor: is used in research, best practice would dictate to mention the use of this tool

units.why: The US Copyright Office position that AI-generated texts "are not eligible for copyright protection" concerns ownership of AI output: P52.
units.anchor: texts and images solely or primarily generated by AI are not eligible for copyright protection

units.why: The Copyright Office guidance "gives instructions on filling out the copyright registration forms to acknowledge the role of AI", another ownership and IP fact: P52.
units.anchor: instructions on filling out the copyright registration forms to acknowledge the role of AI

units.why: "Instructors should practice caution when permitting students to rely on AI for evidence-based assignments" because AI may be wrong: P31, addressed to instructors.
units.anchor: Instructors should practice caution when permitting students to rely on AI for evidence-based assignments

units.why: The guide notes "ChatGPT has been known to fabricate references for sources": AI output can be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: ChatGPT has been known to fabricate references for sources

notes: Coder B. No CS-specific or school-level policy found (per collect file). Regulation REG01.06.03 is about institutional data, not coursework. The library guide reproduces ChatGPT-generated text (assignment ideas, Q&A); those units are coded as informs. Phishing/security unit marked UNCOVERED.
